# Database Overview

## Sports
This is the largest part of the database, covering American football, soccer, baseball, basketball, hockey, cricket, rugby, boxing, Australian rules football, and college football. Common themes are game-day live blogs, weekly previews, rankings, and roster or coaching news. Notable items include fantasy football tight-end rankings for Week 14 (Travis Kelce, T.J. Hockenson, George Kittle) and NFL roundups covering the Lions' 9-3 start, the Rams' Puka Nacua milestone, and the Browns' Joe Flacco debut. Game coverage includes Bills vs. Bengals on Sunday Night Football, Patriots vs. Broncos on Christmas Eve, and Warriors vs. Kings in the NBA In-Season Tournament. Soccer material covers Manchester United's European exit to Bayern Munich, Ten Hag's pressure, Bournemouth's win at Nottingham Forest, the USMNT's October 2023 roster (Gio Reyna's return under Gregg Berhalter), Inter Miami without Lionel Messi, and Argentina's CONMEBOL qualifiers. Other coverage includes the 2023 World Series (Diamondbacks vs. Rangers), MLB free agency (Shohei Ohtani, Kirby Yates), the IPL 2024 auction in Dubai, the West Indies vs. England T20 series, the India vs. Australia ODI World Cup history, Canelo Alvarez vs. Jermell Charlo, and Michigan's sign-stealing penalties and Michigan State's hire of Jonathan Smith. Sports betting appears too, through a Vermont FanDuel launch offer and Canadian odds listings. (Approximately 35% of the database.)

## Consumer Shopping and Product Reviews
This section consists of Black Friday and Cyber Monday deal roundups and buying guides from Verge, Engadget, Wired, and similar outlets. Specific items include PlayStation DualSense controllers at $50, Sony WF-1000XM5 earbuds at $248, Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones, Samsung Galaxy Buds 2 Pro, Apple AirPods Pro (USB-C), and MacBook Pro M3 models. Retailer price-match policies for Google, Home Depot, Best Buy, Target, and Walmart are also covered. Product reviews include the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and their privacy LED, Teenage Engineering's K.O. II sampler, and the Apple 16-inch M3 Max MacBook Pro. Other items are a kids' holiday gift guide, microSD card recommendations, and a cash-back credit card review. (Approximately 12% of the database.)

## Artificial Intelligence
Coverage focuses on generative AI's business effects, regulation, and governance. Key items include the first anniversary of ChatGPT (100 million monthly users within two months of its November 2022 launch), and the OpenAI board's firing of Sam Altman, with Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever involved. The EU AI Act's rules for general-purpose AI, including watermarking obligations and a changeable compute threshold, are covered. Google's Gemini launch was criticized for a faked demo, and Google's US Copyright Office filing on AI training was contrasted with Universal Music Group's stance. YouTube's "Dream Track" voice-cloning trial drew Sony Music's non-participation. Other material includes VC views on AI startup defensibility, AI predictions for 2024, the history of DeepMind and Google, and Boston Dynamics' roots in MIT's Leg Lab. (Approximately 9% of the database.)

## Tech Platforms, Internet and Creator Economy
This section covers social networks, search, and online services. X (formerly Twitter) appears in EU disinformation findings, with penalties of up to 6% of global turnover under the DSA, and in its plan to charge a $1 annual fee and use ID verification against bots. Other items include Snap Map's Gaza coverage and its heat-map restrictions, Google and Apple limits on live traffic in Israel and Gaza, and TikTok's test of a $4.99 ad-free tier. Gmail's new bulk-sender rules and the fediverse (Mastodon, Pixelfed, Lemmy, PeerTube) are discussed. Creator platforms are represented by Twitch's revenue split controversy and competition from YouTube and Kick, Roblox CEO David Baszucki's billion-player goal, and Dropout's farewell to CollegeHumor. An investigation of SEO practices, "The people who ruined the internet," is also included.

## Legal Cases and Courts
The FTX fraud trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is covered through testimony about Gary Wang's code and the defense's objections. Epic Games v. Google is a jury trial, which is distinct from the Apple case, which was a bench trial, and the consolidated US v. Google antitrust trial covers revenue-share deals with Verizon and Samsung and Expedia's complaints about search ads. Uber faces consolidated sexual assault lawsuits before Judge Charles Breyer, and Uber's terms of use bar class actions in these cases. A profile covers a stalker who targeted professors and the Title IX responses at their schools.

## Entertainment, Film and Music
Film coverage includes a horror recommendations list (Jordan Peele's *Us*, with Lupita Nyong'o and Elizabeth Moss) and a guide to *Five Nights at Freddy's*, directed by Emma Tammi and released simultaneously in theaters and on Peacock. Other pieces cover streaming comedy availability (*Wheels on Meals*), the Sphere venue in Las Vegas, and Taylor Swift's NFL presence at Chiefs games, including her possible ties to Travis Kelce. Don McLean's comments on "American Pie," "Silent Night," and his Music City Walk of Fame induction are also covered, along with AfroFuture's growth from Afrochella in Accra.

## Video Games and Tabletop Gaming
This section includes game recommendations and industry news. Tabletop RPG coverage features Monsterhearts, Mörk Borg, and a list of the best games of 2023. Nintendo Switch guidance recommends *Breath of the Wild*, *Tears of the Kingdom*, and *Animal Crossing: New Horizons*. Baldur's Gate 3 class and feat guides cover Warlock builds, and Diablo 4's Season 2 covers Echo of Duriel, Nightmare Dungeons, and quality-of-life changes. Industry context includes Tencent's stakes in companies such as Epic, Ubisoft, and Riot Games, and 2023 layoffs at Epic Games (870 people) and Naughty Dog.

## Business, Markets and Corporate News
Financial coverage includes Hipgnosis Songs Fund's dispute with its valuer Citrin Cooperman and its manager, the blocked Blackstone-linked bid, and JP Morgan's analysis. Market reports cover the ASX, Wall Street's near-20-month high, and China's economic worries. Other items include Flexport's talks to acquire Convoy's technology and its layoffs, Ola Electric's $384 million funding round led by Temasek, and a list of 2023 tech layoffs (Qualtrics cut 780 roles and Chainalysis cut about 15%). Pharma investment analysis covers Biogen and Eisai's Leqembi forecast of $7 billion in peak sales by 2030.

## Science, Health and Environment
Research coverage includes the "pattern effect" in climate sensitivity, which was developed at a 2022 US CLIVAR workshop in Boulder. A study on aqueous zinc-iodine batteries describes a hydrogel electrolyte (Advanced Materials, 2023). Health reports include fasting-mimicking diets and Alzheimer's (Valter Longo and a UC San Diego study), the AIDS epidemic and its end-by-2030 targets, and a mysterious dog respiratory illness. Other items include the Daylight Saving Time debate in the UK and a 2019 YouGov poll.

## Geopolitics and the Israel–Gaza Conflict
This section covers the war with Hamas and the financial and technological responses to it. Israel's Ostrovitch-Levi and the IMPA unit are described as tracing Hamas money flows from abroad, and reports note that most of Hamas's funding is raised globally. Other reports cover how Israel's defense relied on technology before October 7 (published by Globes on November 5, 2023) and how Snap Map remained live to document conditions in Gaza.

## Lifestyle, Celebrity and Human Interest
Celebrity and personal stories include Jada Pinkett Smith and Will Smith's separation since 2016 and the debate over whether couples should divorce. Community stories include the Connecticut "Mombies" who dance to raise money for the Cancer Couch Foundation, and a breast cancer survivor's weight loss story. Travel features cover Northern Lights viewing in the UK (Yorkshire Dales and Northumberland) and luxury ski resorts in Zermatt and Megève.

---

The database is dominated by sports coverage, followed by consumer deals, AI, and tech platform reporting, with smaller shares devoted to entertainment, gaming, business, science, legal matters, and lifestyle. Most items are dated to 2023 and early 2024, reflecting news and commentary from the period around the close of 2023.

[People are turning to Snap Map for firsthand perspectives from Gaza]
Snap Map is especially relevant as other mapping sites limit features in the region at the request of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF). Google disabled live traffic conditions in Israel and the Gaza Strip for Google Maps and Waze last week, Bloomberg reports, “out of consideration for the safety of local communities.” Users can still use navigational features to get around, but aren’t able to see real-time traffic data, according to Bloomberg, because live updates could reveal the Israeli military’s movements. The Hill reports that Apple Maps took similar action in compliance with the IDF’s request.
The company isn’t indifferent to geopolitical conflict, however. Last year, Snap disabled its heat map in Ukraine as a “safety precaution,” The Verge said, to prevent Russia from tracking civilian evacuations. Instead, Snap displayed a “curated feed” of public Stories.
A spokesperson for Snap told TechCrunch that Snap Map will stay live to allow users to continue sharing their experiences during the crisis, and that the company is monitoring hot spots for content that may spread misinformation or incite violence. Snap will “closely assess” if it needs to take additional action.
The spokesperson also acknowledged that Snap Map is a crucial resource for “authentic user-generated content” from perspectives that may not be reflected by traditional news outlets.

[Today the FTX jury suffered through a code review]
As a result of today’s testimony, I am both more and less confused. I am clearer on what probably happened at FTX. What I don’t understand is why Gary Wang did it.
Wang was the co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX, as well as the co-founder of Alameda Research. He owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX. He got a $200,000 a year salary, with no performance bonuses. (Okay, sure, at times he was a billionaire on paper.) By contrast, Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX.
Yet Wang’s testimony suggests he took bizarre risks for his own relatively small share. Bankman-Fried didn’t code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors. Meanwhile, Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim: that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX’s funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. I cannot for the life of me understand why.
